title: Utilitarianism in Professional Relationships
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The article profiles a specific relational type: colleagues who treat professional relationships purely as instruments for personal benefit while pretending otherwise. It argues these "utilitarian mercenaries" eventually get found out because their relationships stay shallow and transactional despite surface effort to appear invested. The piece explores why the pattern is so hard to change — utilitarians are often unable to recognize their own self-interest as the driver of their behavior — and how it corrodes the trust and goodwill others extend to them. It closes with a pragmatic coping strategy for people stuck dealing with a utilitarian colleague: find mutual benefit rather than expecting authentic connection.
points: Utilitarian colleagues mask self-interested motives because of the social stigma attached to being openly transactional, but the mask rarely holds over time.
Their relationships stay 'shallow, underdeveloped, and transactional' because sacrifice and long-term loyalty never factor into their calculus.
A 'coin-operated' orientation toward compensation and reward specifically undermines the goodwill others are willing to extend.
The most workable response isn't confrontation but identifying mutual benefits, since utilitarians respond predictably to what serves their own interests.
quotes: By prioritizing personal benefits over personal attachments and emotions, these utilitarian mercenaries don’t develop authentic or rich relationships with others.
They have learned to pretend to care about others while they secretly focus only on their own desired outcomes.
Over time, people sniff out the fraud of utilitarians, many of whom can’t admit, even to themselves, that their self-interest drives everything they do in relationships.
Their “coin-operated” mentality makes everything they do about what they can get paid. This destroys the goodwill others need to support, help, and collaborate with them.
Ironically, the only way to deal effectively with a utilitarian is to act in kind.
